params.question: A patient with a tibial plateau fracture develops severe pain on passive toe extension and a compartment pressure ΔP of 22 mmHg. Four-compartment fasciotomy of the leg is indicated. Which operative approach is correct?

answers.text: A single anterolateral incision that sequentially releases all four compartments

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A single incision cannot safely access all four compartments of the leg. Two separate longitudinal incisions are required to decompress the anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, and deep posterior compartments.

answers.text: An anteromedial incision for the anterior compartment and a posterolateral incision for the remaining three compartments

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The standard placement is anterolateral (between the fibula and tibial crest) and posteromedial (2 cm posterior to the tibial border) — not anteromedial and posterolateral. Each incision decompresses exactly two compartments.

answers.text: An anterolateral incision for the anterior and lateral compartments, and a posteromedial incision for the superficial and deep posterior compartments

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The anterolateral incision (between the fibula and tibial crest) decompresses the anterior and lateral compartments; the posteromedial incision (2 cm posterior to the tibial border) decompresses the superficial and deep posterior compartments. Both are left open for delayed closure.

answers.text: Medial and lateral incisions placed directly over the tibial crest and fibular shaft respectively

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incisions directly over the subcutaneous tibial crest risk skin necrosis and wound complications. The standard anterolateral incision is placed between the fibula and the tibial crest, not directly over either bone.

overallFeedback.feedback: The standard approach uses two longitudinal incisions: an anterolateral incision (between the fibula and tibial crest) for the anterior and lateral compartments, and a posteromedial incision (2 cm posterior to the tibial border) for the superficial and deep posterior compartments.

Correct! The standard four-compartment fasciotomy uses two longitudinal incisions — anterolateral and posteromedial — each decompressing two compartments. Both incisions are left open for delayed primary closure or split-thickness skin grafting.

interactions.label: Indirect twisting forces on the leg typically produce transverse or short obliqu

params.question: Indirect twisting forces on the leg typically produce transverse or short oblique fractures of the tibia.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Indirect twisting forces produce long spiral or oblique fractures, not transverse ones. Transverse or short oblique fractures result from direct trauma. This mechanism-to-pattern correlation is clinically important because it predicts fracture stability and the degree of associated soft tissue injury.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well identified! Indirect twisting forces produce long spiral or oblique fractures, not transverse ones. It is direct trauma — such as a road traffic accident or direct blow — that produces transverse or short oblique fractures with variable comminution.

interactions.label: A patient sustains a transverse fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction

params.question: A patient sustains a transverse fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal, approximately 1.5 cm distal to the styloid process. Which statement about this injury is most accurate?

answers.text: This is a pseudo-Jones fracture — a peroneus brevis avulsion — managed conservatively with a firm shoe for 4–6 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pseudo-Jones (avulsion) fracture occurs at the very tip of the styloid process, where the peroneus brevis tendon inserts — not at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction. It has a benign course and heals reliably with supportive footwear.

answers.text: This is a stress fracture of the metatarsal neck, commonly seen in marathon runners

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stress (march) fractures typically affect the 2nd or 3rd metatarsal neck or shaft in runners. A transverse fracture at the fifth metatarsal base following acute injury is a Jones fracture, not a stress fracture.

answers.text: This is a Lisfranc fracture-dislocation requiring urgent operative reduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lisfranc injuries involve disruption of the tarsometatarsal joint complex. A fracture at the fifth metatarsal metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction is a Jones fracture — anatomically and prognostically a completely different entity.

answers.text: This is a Jones fracture with a high risk of non-union, requiring close follow-up or surgical fixation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Jones fracture occurs at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal (1.5–2 cm distal to the base), a watershed zone with precarious blood supply. This gives it a high non-union rate, often necessitating prolonged non-weight-bearing or surgical fixation.

overallFeedback.feedback: A transverse fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal (1.5–2 cm distal to the base) is a Jones fracture. Unlike the benign pseudo-Jones avulsion at the styloid tip, the Jones fracture occurs in a watershed vascular zone, giving it a high non-union rate that often requires surgical fixation.

Correct! The Jones fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction has a high non-union rate due to its watershed blood supply — distinguishing it from the benign pseudo-Jones avulsion at the styloid tip. This two-zone distinction is a key clinical pearl for fifth metatarsal injuries.

interactions.label: Which of the following correctly describes the two-phase pathophysiology of fat

params.question: Which of the following correctly describes the two-phase pathophysiology of fat embolism syndrome following a femoral shaft fracture?

answers.text: Both phases are purely mechanical — fat globules first obstruct pulmonary capillaries, then reach cerebral capillaries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Only the first phase is mechanical. The second phase is biochemical — circulating free fatty acids trigger an inflammatory cascade that causes endothelial damage, explaining the delayed, multi-organ nature of FES beyond simple capillary obstruction.

answers.text: In the mechanical phase, bone marrow fat globules enter disrupted venous sinusoids and embolise systemically; in the biochemical phase, free fatty acids trigger an inflammatory cascade causing endothelial damage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Fat globules (>8 µm) are forced into disrupted intramedullary venous sinusoids during fracture or intramedullary manipulation (mechanical phase). They traverse pulmonary capillaries — or pass through a patent foramen ovale — to reach the systemic circulation. The biochemical phase then amplifies the injury through free fatty acid-mediated inflammation.

answers.text: The mechanical phase involves free fatty acid-mediated inflammation; the biochemical phase involves physical obstruction by fat globules

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two phases. The mechanical phase is the physical entry of fat globules into the venous circulation; the biochemical phase is the subsequent inflammatory cascade triggered by free fatty acids released from those globules.

answers.text: The mechanical phase involves air entering fractured bone marrow; the biochemical phase involves platelet aggregation around air bubbles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fat embolism involves fat globules from bone marrow, not air. Air embolism is a distinct clinical entity with different pathophysiology. In FES, bone marrow fat — not air — enters the disrupted venous sinusoids.

overallFeedback.feedback: FES pathophysiology has two phases: a mechanical phase, where bone marrow fat globules (>8 µm) are forced into disrupted intramedullary venous sinusoids; and a biochemical phase, where circulating free fatty acids trigger an inflammatory cascade causing endothelial damage. Understanding both phases explains the progressive, multi-organ nature of the syndrome.

Correct! FES involves a mechanical phase (fat globules from bone marrow enter the venous circulation) followed by a biochemical phase (free fatty acids trigger inflammatory endothelial damage). This dual mechanism explains both the early pulmonary symptoms and the delayed systemic manifestations.
